pages.name: Pressure as a height
pages.text: A column of seawater h metres tall presses ρgh on its base. So any pressure reads as a height. This gauge reads 100 kPa. That holds up 100,000 ÷ (1025 × 9.81), about 9.9 m of seawater. That height is [[head]]. The open tube is a simple [[manometer]]. A pump's head is the height it can raise the liquid. Head is also energy. Lifting 1 N through 1 m takes 1 J. So each metre of head gives 1 J to every newton of liquid.

pages.name: Two gauges
pages.text: A [[U-tube manometer]] is a bent tube, part-filled with liquid. One leg joins the pipe. The other is open to the air. Pressure pushes the liquid down one leg and up the other. The gap between the levels is the pressure, as a head of that liquid. A [[Bourdon gauge]] hides a flattened tube, bent into a C. Pressure makes it straighten a little. Its tip turns the needle. Both read gauge pressure, the pressure above the air around them.

pages.name: Gauges to head
pages.task: A pump moves seawater. Its outlet gauge reads 200 kPa more than its inlet gauge. What head is that?
pages.why: Head is the pressure ÷ ρg. 200 kPa is 200,000 Pa. So the head is 200,000 ÷ (1025 × 9.81), about 19.9 m of seawater. Fresh water is lighter, so the same pressure would hold up a little more of it.

pages.name: Before the friction bar
pages.task: Seawater runs through a pipe at 5 L/s. Then the flow through the same pipe doubles. What happens to the friction head?
pages.why: Twice the flow through the same pipe means twice the speed. The energy each cubic metre of water carries grows with the speed squared. Eddies turn a share of it into heat. So twice the speed loses four times as much.

pages.name: Friction on top
pages.text: Now the water flows. The upper bar is the [[friction head]], the energy lost on the way. In eddying flow it grows with the speed squared. At 5 L/s it is about 2.5 m. At 10 L/s it is about 10.0 m. The lift bar never moves. The left stack is the same pipe at half the flow. The flow ends at 10 L/s, four times the friction of 5 L/s.

pages.name: Darcy's rule
pages.text: [[Darcy's rule]] gives the friction head: f × (L ÷ D) × v² ÷ 2g. L is the pipe's length and D its bore, both in metres. v is the water's speed. f is the [[friction factor]], set mostly by how rough the pipe is. Here it is held at 0.02. A real f shifts a little with speed. Take 50 m of 50 mm pipe at 2 m/s. L ÷ D is 1000. So the loss is 0.02 × 1000 × 2² ÷ 19.62, about 4.1 m.

pages.name: A longer pipe
pages.task: 50 m of 50 mm pipe loses about 4.1 m of head at 2 m/s. How much does 150 m of the same pipe lose at the same speed?
pages.why: The friction grows in step with the length, and with the speed squared. Here only the length changes. Three times the pipe at the same speed loses three times as much, about 12.2 m.

pages.name: The system curve
pages.text: Add the lift and the friction at every flow, and you get the [[system curve]]. Each flow drops a dot at the head it needs. The curve starts at the lift and bends upward as the flow squared. Mostly lift gives a flat curve. Mostly friction gives a steep one. Here the dots run from 0 to 12 L/s.

pages.task: A system has a lift of 10 m and loses 4 m to friction at 5 L/s. What head does it need at 10 L/s?
pages.why: The lift stays 10 m at any flow. Twice the flow gives four times the friction, so 4 × 4 = 16 m. Add them, and 10 + 16 = 26 m.

pages.name: Head to power
pages.text: Each second the pump moves Q cubic metres of water. They weigh ρgQ newtons. It raises each newton through H metres of head. So the water gets ρgQH watts, the [[hydraulic power]]. 10 L/s is 0.01 m³/s. With 20.0 m of head, that is about 2.01 kW. The pump wastes some, so at 70% its shaft must give about 2.87 kW. The motor wastes some too. At 90% it draws about 3.19 kW. Each efficiency divides.

pages.task: The hydraulic power is 2.01 kW and the pump's efficiency is 70%. What power must the shaft give?
pages.why: The pump wastes some of what its shaft gives it. So the shaft must give more than the water gets. Divide by the efficiency: 2.01 ÷ 0.7 is about 2.87 kW.

pages.name: A new pump
pages.task: A pump sends 5 L/s of seawater up a lift of 12 m. The pipe loses 3 m to friction, and the pump's efficiency is 75%. What power must the shaft give?
pages.why: The head is the lift plus the friction, 12 + 3 = 15 m. 5 L/s is 0.005 m³/s. So the water gets 1025 × 9.81 × 0.005 × 15, about 754 W. The shaft must give more: 754 ÷ 0.75 is about 1.01 kW.

pages.name: Half the bore
pages.task: The same flow runs through the same length of pipe. A 100 mm bore is swapped for a 50 mm one. How many times the friction head does that give?
pages.why: Half the bore has a quarter of the area. So the same flow goes four times as fast, and that squared is 16. The length ÷ the bore also doubles. So the friction grows 2 × 16 = 32 times. At 10 L/s through 70 m, about 1.16 m becomes about 37.0 m.
